title: Orphaned canary pinlock recovery and rollout hardening
creator: Arjun Rao
description: Summary: During a routine canary rollout for the text-generation-2 model family we observed a partial rollback that failed to fully unpin canary routes from a small subset of frontend proxies. The leftover pinning caused ~4k concurrent requests to continue hitting an older model variant on a limited dedicated pool, causing queueing and CPU/GPU contention and a brief SLO breach for 18 minutes. The incident combined a subtle routing normalization bug (header normalization + cookie-based routing) with a rollback path that did not emit an explicit 'unpin' marker for route translators, so some proxies retained a cached pin state and continued serving canary traffic after the control plane believed the canary at 0%.
timeline_highlights:
- 2026-02-10 09:18 UTC: Canary rollout started (weight 5%).
- 2026-02-10 09:43 UTC: Observability alert: increase in tail latency for model text-gen-2-alpha.
- 2026-02-10 09:50 UTC: On-call rolled canary back to 0% due to error-rate regression in A/B tests.
- 2026-02-10 09:52 UTC: Control plane reported rollback complete.
- 2026-02-10 10:05 UTC: Several edge proxies still showed active route pins; traffic to pinned variant spiked local dedicated pool.
- 2026-02-10 10:12 UTC: Autoscaler for dedicated pool triggered scale-up but missed capacity due to quota fragmentation; queue grew causing client timeouts.
- 2026-02-10 10:36 UTC: Manual evacuation runbook executed; route pin purge and proxy restart reduced stray traffic.
- 2026-02-10 10:52 UTC: SLOs recovered and alerts cleared.
root_cause: Two factors in combination: (1) a header normalization change introduced in routing v3 that caused the header-based A/B matcher to produce a different identity token on a small subset of proxies, which prevented the rollback command (which matched on the normalized identity) from finding the pinned routes; (2) the rollback implementation relied on a best-effort 'decrement weight' operation without an explicit unpin/unregister step, so proxies that maintained a cached pin state were not reconciled until a full reconciliation cycle or restart.
detection_and_mitigation:
Detection: alerts came from the per-route tail latency monitors and unexpected model variant metrics (variant_x86_old had an uptick).
Immediate mitigation: 1) We executed the emergency runbook to purge pinned route entries from affected proxies and restarted the proxy service on the three noisy hosts. 2) We temporarily shifted traffic via region-level routing to divert requests away from the impacted dedicated pool. 3) We applied a quick control-plane patch to emit an explicit 'unpin' command for subsequent rollback attempts.
Outcome: Recovery took 18 minutes from rollback command to full reconvergence. No data loss; client retries observed but error budget consumed for the window.
postmortem_conclusions:
- Rollback must be an explicit state transition (pin -> unpin) rather than relying on weight arithmetic.
- Routing config convergence relies on deterministic normalization; changes to normalization rules must be gate-kept with multi-proxy canary and a reconciliation smoke test.
- Autoscaler fragmentation can prevent timely buffer capacity; we need a reserved emergency headroom policy for critical dedicated pools when rollbacks occur.

AI-2: Add reconciliation ack from proxies: rollback should require acknowledgement from >95% of edge proxies or escalate (owner: Leo Martinez, due: 2026-03-03)

notes: This incident surfaced a class of determinism/regression issues between control plane and edge proxies. Priority is to make rollbacks reproducible and observable across the fleet. The solution path favors explicit state transitions and stronger ack/health checks over implicit arithmetic operations.
